facts.text: On 18 November 1995 the second applicant was arrested and taken into police custody on suspicion of membership of an illegal armed organisation, namely the PKK.

facts.text: The first applicant was arrested and detained on 23 November 1995 on suspicion of membership of the PKK.

anchor.surface_text: 5.  On 18 November 1995 the second applicant was arrested and taken into police custody on suspicion of membership of an illegal armed organisation, namely the PKK (Workers’ Party of Kurdistan). The first applicant was arrested and detained, on 23 November 1995, on the same grounds.

facts.text: On 24 November 1995 the applicants and two other suspects were identified as responsible by eyewitnesses Mr G.T. and Mr O.T. for the killing of their father, Mr M.S.T., by the PKK.

anchor.surface_text: 6.  On 24 November 1995 the applicants and two other suspects were identified as those responsible by Mr G.T. and Mr O.T., eyewitnesses to the killing of their father, Mr M.S.T., by the PKK.

facts.text: On 26 November 1995 the applicants were interrogated by two police officers in the absence of a lawyer and gave detailed statements regarding their participation in the killing of Mr M.S.T and kidnapping of G.T. on behalf of the PKK.

anchor.surface_text: 7.  On 26 November 1995 the applicants were interrogated by two police officers, in the absence of a lawyer, and they both gave detailed statements regarding their participation in, inter alia, the killing of Mr M.S.T and kidnapping of G.T., on 2 August 1995, on behalf of the PKK.

facts.text: On 27 November 1995 the applicants, without a lawyer, identified a deceased suspect from photos and were confronted with other suspects, giving details about other detainees.

anchor.surface_text: 8.  On 27 November 1995 the applicants, in the absence of a lawyer, were first asked to identify from photos a deceased suspect and later confronted with other suspects. During this procedure both applicants gave details about the other detainees, such as their code names and acts undertaken by them.

facts.text: On 28 November 1995 at 10.25 a.m. a doctor examined the applicants and noted the first applicant had a bruise on his lower lip and the second had scratches on his knee and back pain.

anchor.surface_text: 9.  On 28 November 1995, at 10.25 a.m., the applicants were examined by a doctor who noted that the first applicant had a bruise of 1x1 cm on his lower lip and that the second applicant had two scratches of 2 cm on his lower right knee and pain in his back and lower back.

facts.text: The applicants claimed in their application form that they had been subjected to ill-treatment in police custody including electric shocks, falaka, and Palestinian hanging.

anchor.surface_text: 10.  In their application form the applicants submitted that they had been subjected to ill-treatment while in police custody. In this connection, they claimed that they had received electric shocks, falaka (beating of the soles of the feet) and Palestinian hanging.

facts.text: In a letter dated 5 October 2004 the first applicant detailed alleged ill-treatment during arrest and police custody including beatings, electric shocks, and threats.

anchor.surface_text: 11.  In a letter to the Court dated 5 October 2004 the first applicant submitted, inter alia, that during his arrest he and his family had been sworn at and threatened and that when they had arrived at the police station he had been blindfolded. Subsequently, he had been interrogated by five or six police officers who had kicked and punched him and hit him with sticks. One of them had hit him in the stomach and another had stood on his head. When he had denied the accusations, they had subjected him to hanging and to electric shocks on his penis and feet. Later, when he had refused to sign a statement written by the police, two police officers had punched him in the face and squeezed his penis. Because of the pain he had signed the statement. The applicant further stated that the doctor who had examined him had seen the swelling on his lips and penis and had decided to transfer him to hospital but that the relevant paper had been ripped up by the police.

facts.text: On 24 November 1995 the applicants were brought before the public prosecutor at the Istanbul State Security Court and refused to give any statements.

anchor.surface_text: 12.  On the same day the applicants were brought before the public prosecutor at the Istanbul State Security Court where they refused to give any statements.

facts.text: On 24 November 1995 the applicants were brought before a judge at the State Security Court, refuted their police statements, and were remanded in custody.

anchor.surface_text: 13.  Later that same day the applicants were brought before a judge at the State Security Court where they refuted the contents of their statements to the police. The second applicant claimed that some of these submissions had been written by the police and that he had made others under duress. The first applicant submitted that the police had made him sign the statement without reading it. The judge remanded them in custody.

facts.text: On 5 December 1995 the public prosecutor indicted the applicants under Article 125 of the Criminal Code for activities aimed at secession, including participation in killing and kidnapping on 2 August 1995.

anchor.surface_text: 14.  On 5 December 1995 the public prosecutor at the Istanbul State Security Court indicted the applicants under Article 125 of the Criminal Code for engaging in activities for the purpose of bringing about the secession of part of the national territory. In particular, they were accused of participating in the killing of Mr M.S.T and kidnapping of G.T. on 2 August 1995.

facts.text: Between 5 March 1996 and 2 July 1999 the court held regular hearings examining accused and witnesses, including defense witnesses.

anchor.surface_text: 17.  Between 5 March 1996 and 2 July 1999 the court held hearings on a regular basis during which it examined the accused and a number of witnesses, including those appearing for the defence.

facts.text: On 18 June 1999 the Constitution was amended and military judges on State security courts were replaced by civilian judges.

anchor.surface_text: 18.  On 18 June 1999 the Constitution was amended and the military judges on the bench of the State security courts were replaced by civilian judges.

facts.text: On 2 July 1999 the military judge was replaced by a civilian judge who sat as a member of the trial court for the first time.

anchor.surface_text: 19.  At a hearing on 2 July 1999 the judge who had been appointed to replace the military judge sat as a member of the trial court for the first time.

facts.text: On 17 November 1999 the court convicted the applicants under Article 168 of the Criminal Code and sentenced them to twelve years and six months’ imprisonment.

anchor.surface_text: 22.  On 17 November 1999 the court held a hearing. On the same day it decided to convict the applicants under, inter alia, Article 168 of the Criminal Code and sentenced them to twelve years and six months’ imprisonment.

facts.text: On 20 June 2000 the first applicant complained to the Human Rights Commission of the Turkish Grand National Assembly about alleged ill-treatment.

anchor.surface_text: 23.  In the meantime, on 20 June 2000, the first applicant wrote to Ms Pişkinsüt, the chair of the Human Rights Commission of the Turkish Grand National Assembly, complaining about his alleged ill‑treatment.

facts.text: On 12 June 2001 the Fatih public prosecutor’s office decided not to prosecute any police officer due to expiration of the statutory time-limit.

anchor.surface_text: On 12 June 2001 the Fatih public prosecutor’s office decided not to commit any police officer for trial on the ground that the statutory time-limit for prosecution of the offence had expired.

facts.text: On 20 December 2000 the applicants appealed, submitting that their conviction was based on statements obtained under duress.

anchor.surface_text: 24.  On 20 December 2000 the applicants appealed. In their petition they submitted, inter alia, that the first-instance court had based its conviction on their statements in police custody which had been obtained under duress.

facts.text: On 1 February 2001 the Court of Cassation upheld the first-instance court's judgment concerning the applicants’ conviction and sentence.

anchor.surface_text: 25.  On 1 February 2001 the Court of Cassation held a hearing and upheld the judgment of the first-instance court in so far as it concerned the applicants’ conviction and sentence.

facts.text: On 9 November 2004 the applicants were released from prison.

Article 6 §§ 1 and 3 (c) of the Convention, of which the relevant part reads as follows:

“1.  In the determination of ... any criminal charge against him, everyone is entitled to a fair ... hearing within a reasonable time by an independent and impartial tribunal established by law.

3.  Everyone charged with a criminal offence has the following minimum rights:

(c) to defend himself in person or through legal assistance of his own choosing or, if he has not sufficient means to pay for legal assistance, to be given it free when the interests of justice so require.”

concepts.interpretation: The Court found violations of Article 6 § 1 due to lack of independence and impartiality of the trial court and of Article 6 § 3 (c) due to denial of access to a lawyer during police custody.

FOR THESE REASONS, THE COURT UNANIMOUSLY

1.  Declares the complaints concerning the alleged ill-treatment of the applicants and their right to a fair hearing by an independent and impartial tribunal admissible and the remainder of the application inadmissible;

holdings.reasoning_summary: The Court found the complaints admissible for examination and declared the rest inadmissible, allowing the case to proceed on key issues.

holdings.text: Holds that there has been no violation of Article 3 of the Convention under its substantive limb

anchor.surface_text: 2.  Holds that there has been no violation of Article 3 of the Convention under its substantive limb;

holdings.reasoning_summary: The Court found insufficient evidence beyond reasonable doubt to conclude that the applicants were subjected to ill-treatment reaching the severity threshold of Article 3.

holdings.text: Holds that there has been a violation of Article 3 of the Convention under its procedural limb

anchor.surface_text: 3.  Holds that there has been a violation of Article 3 of the Convention under its procedural limb;

holdings.reasoning_summary: The Court held that the State failed to conduct an effective investigation into arguable allegations of ill-treatment as required by Article 3.

holdings.text: Holds that there has been a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention as regards the lack of independence and impartiality of the Istanbul State Security Court

anchor.surface_text: 4.   Holds that there has been a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention as regards the lack of independence and impartiality of the Istanbul State Security Court;

holdings.reasoning_summary: The Court found that the participation of a military judge compromised the independence and impartiality of the trial court, violating Article 6 § 1.

holdings.text: Holds that there has been a violation of Article 6 § 1 in conjunction with Article 6 § 3 (c) of the Convention

anchor.surface_text: 5.  Holds that there has been a violation of Article 6 § 1 in conjunction with Article 6 § 3 (c) of the Convention;

holdings.reasoning_summary: The Court held that the absence of a lawyer during police custody irretrievably affected the applicants' defence rights, violating Article 6 §§ 1 and 3 (c).

holdings.text: Holds that the respondent State is to pay each of the applicants, within three months from the date on which the judgment becomes final in accordance with Article 44 § 2 of the Convention, EUR 6,500 (six thousand five hundred euros), plus any tax that may be chargeable, in respect of non‑pecuniary damage

anchor.surface_text: 4.   Holds that there has been a violation of Article 6 § 1 of the Convention as regards the lack of independence and impartiality of the Istanbul State Security Court;

6.  Holds

(a)  that the respondent State is to pay each of the applicants, within three months from the date on which the judgment becomes final in accordance with Article 44 § 2 of the Convention, EUR 6,500 (six thousand five hundred euros), plus any tax that may be chargeable, in respect of non‑pecuniary damage, to be converted into Turkish liras at the rate applicable at the date of settlement;

(b)  that from the expiry of the above-mentioned three months until settlement simple interest shall be payable on the above amount at a rate equal to the marginal lending rate of the European Central Bank during the default period plus three percentage points;
